Correct option: 2. Once one list empties, every remaining key comes from the other already sorted list. No ordering choice between two heads remains. For example, merging [1,2,3] with [10,11,12] uses three head comparisons and then copies three keys. Those copies are necessary output operations but are not three extra head comparisons.

Option one contradicts the exact linear bound p+q-1 for nonempty inputs. Option three introduces unnecessary comparisons inside an already ordered suffix. Option four mistakes two moving pointers for two independently nested enumeration ranges. The total number of pointer advances cannot exceed the number of available keys.

The operation ledger should distinguish comparisons, reads and writes. With output materialization, exactly p+q keys are written even on a minimum-comparison input. If an implementation repeatedly copies its entire current prefix instead of appending once, its copying cost may be larger, but that is an additional implementation cost rather than a change to the merge's head-comparison theorem. Defining the counted operation prevents both undercharging full runtime and overcharging comparisons.

Integrated multistep challenges

Question 45. Three-factor integer region

Original integrated loop-counting challenge; not an authentic examination item.

Count executions over all positive integer triples (i,j,k) with ijk≤n. Identify the tight growth order, derive the exact finite sum, and give an explicit feasible-region lower witness.

1. Θ(nlogn)

2. Θ(nlog2n)

3. Θ(n2)

4. Θ(n3)

Read the complete operation ledger and mathematical derivation

Correct option: 2. Each positive pair (i,j) with ij≤n admits exactly ⌊n/(ij)⌋ positive choices of k. Hence the exact count is

A(n)=∑i=1n∑j=1⌊n/i⌋⌊nij⌋.

For an upper bound, replace the floor by its argument and enlarge the inner range to 1,…,n, adding only nonnegative terms. This gives A(n)≤nHn2=O(n(lnn)2).

For a matching lower bound, set m=⌊n1/3⌋. All 1≤i,j≤m satisfy ij≤n2/3≤n, so their pairs are feasible. Since n/(ij)≥1, the inequality ⌊x⌋≥x/2 applies. Restricting the exact sum to this square gives

A(n)≥n2∑i=1m∑j=1m1ij=n2Hm2.

For n≥64, m≥n1/3/2. The harmonic lower bound then gives Hm≥ln(m+1)≥(lnn)/3-ln2≥(lnn)/6. Thus A(n)≥n(lnn)2/72, an explicit uniform witness. Both bounds establish the requested tight class.

The first option omits one harmonic aggregation. The quadratic and cubic options overcount the product-constrained region as more rectangular than it is; their ratios to n(lnn)2 diverge. At n=1, the exact count is one, although the asymptotic expression vanishes there; exact boundary values are not supplied by a large-size class. The layer-grid animation shows legal (j,k) pairs separately for fixed i on a small instance, complementing the analytic proof rather than replacing it by a finite plot.

The full mathematical derivation is written above.

Question 46. A branch-defined triangular region

Original integrated loop-counting challenge; not an authentic examination item.

For each i=1,…,n, start j=1 and execute the body while j≤n and i+j≤n, incrementing j each time. Find the exact count. Also count each guard predicate under left-to-right short circuit and normal termination.

1. n(n+1)/2

2. n(n-1)/2

3. n2

4. n-1

Read the complete operation ledger and mathematical derivation

Correct option: 2. For fixed i, the two guard conditions require 1≤j≤n and j≤n-i. Since i≥1, the second is the stronger upper bound. If i=n, no positive j satisfies it. The row lengths are therefore n-1,n-2,…,1,0, and

B=∑i=1n(n-i)=n(n-1)2.

An independent bijection maps (i,j) to (i,s=i+j). The admissible values satisfy 1≤i<s≤n, so they are exactly the two-element subsets of 1,…,n. This gives (n2) and confirms the endpoint convention.

Option one adds one invalid position per outer row. The rectangle n2 ignores the sum constraint. The final option n-1 counts only the first row. At n=1, the entire region is empty; at n=2, it contains only (1,1). Such checks expose a missing empty last row.

For full guard accounting under left-to-right short circuit, j<=n is evaluated n-i+1 times in each row. The last tested value is j=n-i+1≤n, so i+j<=n is also evaluated on every such test; it supplies the terminating false outcome. Both predicate frequencies total B+n=n(n+1)/2, despite only B body visits. This explains why the logical conjunction and body count must not be treated as one undifferentiated operation.

Complete operation-counting rules and examination traps

1. Name the operation being counted

Body calls, key comparisons, guard predicates, assignments and output writes are different quantities. Give the requested ledger first; add other ledgers only when translating that count into full runtime under an explicit cost model.

2. State the domain and arithmetic semantics

Declare nonnegative or positive integer sizes, independent parameters and enough counter capacity. A terminating mathematical-integer loop may wrap or overflow in a concrete language. Its iteration theorem does not automatically transfer to the changed semantics.

3. Count the final false guard

A normal pretest invocation with q bodies has q+1 header evaluations. In a nested loop, add one such final test per inner invocation, including empty rows. A break from inside a body removes the normal final false header test for that invocation.

4. Charge initialization per invocation

An inner loop initialized on every outer row incurs one initialization per row, not per inner body. At zero-size input, setup and a false outer guard can remain even when the chosen body count vanishes.

5. Inspect continue and update placement

A conventional C-style for-loop continues to its update expression after continue. A while-loop update placed later in the body can be bypassed, creating a repeated state and nontermination. The fragments' control flow determines the count.

6. Count short-circuit predicates separately

In P and Q, the right predicate is evaluated only when the left is true. Its final failed evaluation depends on which predicate ends the loop. A composite condition is not necessarily one constant-cost operation.

7. Write the index region

Independent bounds create a rectangular region; dependent bounds require row sums or another exact partition. Replacing all rows by their maximum supplies an upper estimate, not generally an exact count or a matching lower bound.

8. Retain inclusive and strict endpoints

Starting at zero with fixed positive step d, the guard j<M gives ⌈M/d⌉ visits, while j<=M gives ⌊M/d⌋+1. Changing one endpoint can affect every row in a nested program.

9. Distinguish weak and strict order

Strict triples count (n3), weak triples count (n+23), and i≤j<k counts (n+13). Shift to strict positions and construct the inverse map to justify each formula rather than guessing a factorial division.

10. Check equality cases explicitly

Weak triples split into all-distinct, exactly-two-equal and all-equal cases. Their counts are (n3), 2(n2) and n. Equality cases contribute n2 additional triples and cannot be discarded in an exact question.

11. Use row increments as an independent check

A candidate finite count should gain exactly the newly admitted row when the size increases. For squared rows, the increment is n2; for weak triples, it is the number of weak pairs at the new last index.

12. Derive power sums with uniform hypotheses

For fixed p≥0, the last half of the terms proves ∑i=1nip∈Θ(np+1). The witness constant depends on fixed p. If p grows with input, that proof is not uniform and may conceal superpolynomial work.

13. Distinguish geometric stages from their work

The values 1,2,4,…,2h give h+1 visits. Charging the current value per visit gives 2h+1-1 operations. A logarithmic stage count alone does not determine total work.

14. Define the size parameter for exponent schedules

Work 2n+1-1 is exponential in maximum exponent n but linear in final numerical scale N=2n. Neither description is meaningful without naming the input measure and representation.

15. Solve multiplicative guards algebraically

With positive start a and fixed multiplier b>1, inclusive bound M gives ⌊logb(M/a)⌋+1 visits when a≤M. If the start already exceeds the bound, the count is zero; logarithmic formulas must respect this case.

16. Treat zero-start multiplication as a progress defect

Doubling zero does not leave zero. A positive-bound loop started there can run forever. Establish termination before assigning any logarithmic runtime class.

17. Recheck squaring endpoints

Starting at two and squaring visits 22r. Inclusive bound N≥2 gives ⌊log2log2N⌋+1 visits; strict bound gives ⌈log2log2N⌉. Big-integer multiplication cost is separate from this visit count.

18. Count divisibility by multiples

For fixed divisor j, exactly ⌊n/j⌋ positive targets up to n are multiples. Summing those rows counts successful branches; summing divisor counts by target counts the same finite set differently.

19. Preserve floors in exact answers

The successful divisor count is D(n)=∑j=1n⌊n/j⌋. Fractional row lengths are not body visits. The uniform sandwich (n/2)Hn≤D(n)≤nHn proves growth without asserting an exact harmonic value.

20. A rare body does not remove its tests

An all-pairs divisibility implementation makes n2 condition checks even though its successful body count is tight nlogn. Direct multiple stepping changes the implementation ledger while preserving the successful set.

21. Reverse a finite double count when useful

Starting from each positive index and doubling yields ∑t≥0⌊n/2t⌋, not a tight nlogn count. The exact identity is 2n-s2(n), where s2(n) counts one-bits in the binary expansion.

22. A filtered triangle need not split equally

For 1≤j≤i≤n with even i+j, kept rows have ⌈i/2⌉ positions and total ⌊(n+1)2/4⌋. The diagonal is entirely kept, so halving the unfiltered triangle gives the wrong exact count.

23. Count residues with the endpoint included

Skipping multiples of fixed positive d through M leaves M-⌊M/d⌋ bodies. A density approximation may hide the last partial block. With d=1, every index is skipped, so a positive linear success lower bound fails.

24. Expand a variable body into a weighted sum

If each visit (i,j) costs j unit actions, total work is ∑i∑jj, not the number of visits. Integer weights can be interpreted as an extra counting index; otherwise bound the weighted sum directly.

25. Require uniform constants when summing costs

Summing a stated Θ(f(i)) body cost requires uniform positive witnesses over the relevant calls. An O(f(i)) promise alone supplies only an upper bound and does not justify a tight total.

26. Separate input-specific counts from worst cases

A supplied merge array has one exact trace; alternating inputs attain a maximum. A worst-case upper bound need not equal the given instance's count. A maximum claim needs both an upper theorem and an attainable input family.

27. Monotone merge pointers give linear comparisons

For two nonempty inputs of lengths p,q, the maximum head-key comparisons are p+q-1. Appending a leftover sorted suffix needs no head comparison, but output materialization still writes p+q keys.

28. Accumulated lengths determine sequential merging

With k equal lists of length m=n/k, stage j processes jm keys. Summing gives tight nk work for k≥2. Balanced merging has a different schedule and tight nlogk work; do not substitute its theorem for sequential code.

29. Distinguish a branch expectation from scan length

A random-permutation running minimum has expected update count Hn, derived by indicators and linearity. Every element is still compared. A fixed-array trace or a biased distribution does not automatically have that expectation.

30. Restrict a feasible region for lower bounds

For ijk≤n, enlarging a range proves an upper bound, while a square of small outer factors proves a lower bound. The resulting tight n(logn)2 count needs both arguments; counting a full cube ignores feasibility.

31. Retain independent size parameters and overhead

Initializing lengths m,n and traversing all pairs has modeled work proportional to 1+m+n+mn, including constant setup if the origin is part of the claim. Replace dimensions by one parameter only after establishing their relation.

32. Use finite checks to challenge, not certify, proofs

Check zero and one, endpoint powers and adjacent values, actual row increments and independently enumerated small regions. A successful finite trace illustrates its contract. General correctness and growth still require the explicit identities, invariant arguments or uniform bounds written in the solutions.

The source audit distinguishes portions actually read from candidates only screened. The exercises are independently worded and solved rather than copied from course handouts. This chapter covers the named nonrecursive loop patterns and their identified boundary cases; it does not claim to enumerate every program, every university exercise, or every unseen examination problem. Compiler behavior, input/output costs, arbitrary-precision arithmetic, concurrency, caches, and distribution-dependent expected cases require their own models. A strong result on future examination questions depends on practice and verified transfer of these methods, not a literal guarantee of 100% performance.
